name: Hadrian's Wall
info: Hadrian's Wall was a defensive fortification of the Roman province of Britannia, begun in 122 under the emperor Hadrian and running 80 Roman miles across northern England from the River Tyne to the Solway Firth.

facts.made: Begun in 122 in the reign of the emperor Hadrian; built by three Roman legions, the Legio II Augusta, Legio VI Victrix and Legio XX Valeria Victrix, with some members of the Roman fleet, and later garrisoned by auxiliary regiments
facts.form: A stone wall in its final version, with large ditches in front and behind, 80 Roman miles (73 modern miles, 117 kilometres) long, with forts, milecastles and turrets, and a western section first built of turf
facts.where: Entirely within England, from Wallsend on the River Tyne to Bowness-on-Solway; almost all the standing masonry was removed in early modern times, and many excavated forts are open to the public with museums nearby
facts.known: its length across the whole width of the island; forts, milecastles and turrets; the Vallum to the south; the turf wall of the western section; the later Antonine Wall; its reuse as building stone; its preservation by John Clayton; its World Heritage listing

t: Hadrian ended Trajan's policy of expansion and defended the existing borders; Britain had no natural boundary, so a wall was built across the whole width of the island, begun in 122.

The wall was a physical barrier that slowed raiders and channelled movement through gates where it could be monitored and taxed, and it was also a statement of imperial power; scholars differ on how great the threat from the north was.
Roman rule in Britain ended around 410, and the wall fell into ruin; its stone was reused for centuries, and much of what remains owes its preservation to the antiquarian John Clayton.
dyk: A copper alloy pan of the 2nd century, found in Staffordshire in 2003, is inscribed with the names of four forts on the western sector of the wall, followed by words that most likely read as 'Hadrian's Wall', though they may instead name a man called Aelius Draco.
ev: Construction of the wall began in the reign of the emperor Hadrian
Work began on the turf-built Antonine Wall in what is now central Scotland, which briefly superseded Hadrian's Wall
Marcus Aurelius abandoned the Antonine Wall and reoccupied Hadrian's Wall as the main defensive barrier
The estimated end of Roman rule in Britain, after which the wall fell into ruin
Stone reused from the wall was probably built into St Paul's Church at Monkwearmouth-Jarrow before its dedication stone was set
John Clayton began buying land along the wall to stop farmers taking its stones
The wall was declared a World Heritage Site
It became part of the transnational Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage Site

sections.origins:
Hadrian's Wall was a defensive fortification of the Roman province of Britannia, begun in 122 in the reign of the emperor Hadrian. It was probably planned before Hadrian's visit to Britain in 122. Restored sandstone fragments found in Jarrow, dating from 118 or 119, record Hadrian's wish to keep the empire "intact", which had been imposed on him via "divine instruction". On his accession in 117 there was unrest and rebellion in Roman Britain and among the peoples of various conquered lands, including Egypt, Judea, Libya and Mauretania. These troubles may have influenced his plan for the wall, as well as his construction of frontier boundaries known as limes in other areas of the empire, such as the Limes Germanicus in Germany.

Hadrian ended his predecessor Trajan's policy of expanding the empire and focused on defending the current borders, which at the time included Britain. Like Augustus, he believed in exploiting natural boundaries such as rivers, for example the Euphrates, Rhine and Danube. Britain had no natural boundary that could divide the province controlled by the Romans from the Celtic tribes in the north. The route lay slightly north of the Stanegate, an important Roman road built several decades earlier to link two forts that guarded river crossings: Corstopitum (Corbridge) on the Tyne and Luguvalium (Carlisle) on the Eden.
sections.content:
The wall ran for 80 Roman miles, equivalent to 73 modern miles or 117 kilometres, from Segedunum at Wallsend on the River Tyne, via Carlisle and Kirkandrews-on-Eden, to the shore of the Solway Firth, ending a short but unknown distance west of Bowness-on-Solway. In its final version it was a stone wall with large ditches in front and behind, and part of the central section follows natural cliffs on an escarpment of the Whin Sill rock formation. Along it stood large forts, smaller milecastles and, every third of a mile, a watch-tower turret that also gave shelter and living accommodation to troops. The system of milecastles and turrets continued along the Cumbria coast as far as Risehow, south of Maryport.

Just south of the wall lay the Vallum, a deep ditch-like construction with a mound running along each side of it. On the berm in front of the wall were pits known as cippi, which held branches or small tree trunks entangled with sharpened branches, which might be thought of as the Roman equivalent of barbed wire. Movement was channelled through the gates in the wall, where it could be monitored, prevented or permitted as appropriate, and taxed. There is some evidence that the wall was originally covered in plaster and whitewashed.
sections.making:
Construction began in 122, with an alternating series of forts, each housing 600 men, and manned milecastles, operated by "between 12 and 20 men". It took six years to build most of the wall, with the work coming from three legions, the Legio II Augusta, Legio VI Victrix and Legio XX Valeria Victrix, totalling 15,000 soldiers, plus some members of the Roman fleet. Some of the soldiers would have trained as surveyors, engineers, masons and carpenters. Not long after construction began, the planned thickness of 10 feet was reduced to about 8 feet, or less depending on the terrain. R. G. Collingwood cited evidence for a Broad Wall and a Narrow Wall and argued that the plans possibly changed because of a lack of resources.

From Milecastle 49 to Bowness-on-Solway the wall was originally built of turf, possibly because limestone was absent. This turf wall was 6 metres wide at its base and about 3.66 metres high. It was later demolished and replaced in stone, in two phases: the first during Hadrian's reign, the second after the reoccupation that followed the abandonment of the Antonine Wall, though it has also been suggested that the second took place under Septimius Severus. The date of the Vallum was disputed. Collingwood asserted in 1930 that it was built before the wall in its final form, but research in 1936 found that it avoided one of the wall's milecastles, which supported a simultaneous construction.
sections.reception:
Almost 10,000 soldiers are thought to have been stationed on the wall once it was fully manned, drawn not from the legions that built it but from regiments of auxiliary infantry and cavalry from the provinces. David Breeze holds that the troops in the forts had the primary duty of defence, while those in the milecastles and turrets were responsible for frontier control. Scholars differ on the purpose of the wall. Its primary purpose was probably as a physical barrier to slow raiders intent on taking animals, treasure or slaves; it also kept people within the province. Neil Faulkner called it "as much a propaganda statement as a functional facility". In recent years some scholars have questioned how much of a threat the inhabitants of northern Britain presented and whether a fixed line of defences gave any economic advantage.

The wall probably cut across a coherent cultural area. To the south, Roman-style settlements appear in the early 2nd century, very shortly after it was built. To the north a large area of southern Scotland and the Northumbrian coastal plain lost its monumental building tradition, and the Romans may have cleared a zone of its population. Roman coins and pottery generally did not cross the wall, which seems to have been an effective barrier to trade, though exchange may have been managed at a few crossing points. Breeze and B. Dobson suggested that Hadrian may have been influenced by accounts of the Great Wall of China; Duncan B. Campbell argued that a long tradition of wall-building in the Mediterranean world gave a precedent.
sections.survival:
After Hadrian's death in 138, Antoninus Pius left the wall occupied in a support role and began building the turf-built Antonine Wall about 160 kilometres north. Marcus Aurelius abandoned that wall and reoccupied Hadrian's Wall in 164. In 208–211 Septimius Severus again tried to conquer Caledonia and temporarily reoccupied the Antonine Wall; the campaign ended inconclusively and the Romans withdrew to Hadrian's Wall. By 410, the estimated end of Roman rule in Britain, the Roman administration and its legions were gone, though archaeologists have found that some parts of the wall stayed occupied well into the 5th century. The wall fell into ruin and its stone was reused in local buildings; some of it was built into St Paul's Church at Monkwearmouth-Jarrow, where Bede was a monk.

Bede, who died in 735, wrote that the wall was 8 feet broad and 12 feet high, but he appears to have believed that the Vallum was a rampart built by Severus. Almost all the standing masonry was removed in early modern times for local roads and farmhouses, and in the 18th century General Wade used long sections for the military road built to crush the Jacobite rising of 1745. The antiquarian John Clayton, from 1834, bought land along the wall to stop farmers taking its stones, excavated forts and milecastles, and had sections restored to about seven courses. After his death the estate was lost to gambling, and the National Trust began acquiring the land. In 2021 workers found a previously undiscovered 3-metre section in central Newcastle upon Tyne.
sections.legacy:
Hadrian's Wall is the largest Roman archaeological feature in Britain and is regarded as a British cultural icon. It lies entirely within England and has never formed the Anglo-Scottish border, though it is sometimes loosely described as such. It was designated a World Heritage Site in 1987, and in 2005 it became part of the transnational Frontiers of the Roman Empire site, which also includes sites in Germany. The Hadrian's Wall Path, a National Trail, opened in 2003 and follows the line of the wall.

In the Roman period the wall seems to have been called the vallum. Bronze vessels such as the Staffordshire Moorlands Pan, the Rudge Cup, the Amiens Skillet and the Berlanga Cup bear the Latin names of its forts, with a depiction of a battlemented wall beneath, and are thought to have been souvenirs valued by owners who might have been veterans of the auxiliary units there. John Speed called the wall the "Picts Wall" and William Matthew's 1610 map of Newcastle named it "Severus' Wall", following Bede's name for the Vallum. Rudyard Kipling's Puck of Pook's Hill (1906) contributed to the popular image of the "Great Pict Wall", and W. H. Auden wrote a 1937 radio script and the poem "Roman Wall Blues" in the voice of a lonely Roman soldier stationed there.

summary: Hadrian's Wall, begun in 122, was a Roman fortification 80 Roman miles long across northern England, with forts, milecastles and turrets. It was briefly superseded by the Antonine Wall, fell into ruin after Roman rule ended and was quarried for centuries, and much of what survives owes its preservation to John Clayton.
references: David J. Breeze, The hinterland of Hadrian's Wall (Archaeopress, 2023)
notes: Width: the article gives the planned 10 feet reduced to about 8 feet, but Collingwood's broad sections are about nine and a half feet (2.9 m) and narrow ones about seven and a half feet; the text gives only the 10-to-8 figures and the Broad/Narrow terms without numbers.
The Vallum's date is disputed in the article (Collingwood 1930, 1936 research, Couse); only the first two positions are given.
Section lengths: see checker; start 122 is the article's own year for the beginning of building (planning probably earlier).

Left out: the popular culture section (novels, films, television), tourism, the 2010 and 2012 light events and the 2018 agreement with the Great Wall's managers, as barred by the brief; the fort list; the Garrison theories in detail; the Burnswark Hill fort.

The article has the Antonine Wall as 'of AD 142' in the lead; the 142 event follows that. The lead says the Antonine Wall 'briefly superseded' Hadrian's Wall; the body says Antoninus left the wall occupied in a support role, 'essentially abandoning' it.
The 'Roman-period names' section says the wall was known in the Roman period as the vallum; the Staffordshire Moorlands Pan reading is hedged by the article (Aelius Draco is the alternative).
Antonine Wall distance: article says about 160 kilometres north (100 mi).
